analysis.one_liner: Cuts the corporate income tax to a single 20% flat rate with no offsetting revenue.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have cut the top corporate tax rate from 35% to 20%, was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on June 25, 2015 and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would replace the corporate income tax's tiered rates — with a top rate of 35% — with one flat 20% rate on all corporate profits. It contains no spending cuts, tax increases, or other provisions to make up the lost revenue, so the rate cut would be paid for out of the Treasury, reducing federal income by hundreds of billions of dollars over time. The bill never advanced past its referral to committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Profitable corporations, and their shareholders, who would pay substantially less federal tax on profits. The largest savings would go to the biggest and most profitable companies, since they paid the highest rates under the tiered structure this bill deletes.

how_it_helps.text: Replaces the corporate tax's rate schedule with a single 20% tax on all corporate taxable income, cutting the top rate from 35% to 20% effective for tax years beginning after December 31, 2015 [S2] [S3].
Conforms related provisions of the tax code — including withholding on foreign partners and the section 7874 inversion rules — to the new 20% rate [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury and, ultimately, taxpayers generally: the bill raises nothing to replace the revenue the rate cut forgos, so the difference would be added to deficits or made up later through other taxes or spending cuts.

drawbacks.text: The bill contains no revenue offset of any kind; cutting the rate on all corporate taxable income to 20% would substantially reduce federal revenue and add to deficits [S2] [S3].
The largest dollar savings go to the biggest, most profitable corporations, which paid the top 35% rate; small businesses organized as corporations in lower brackets gain proportionally less [S3].

Deficit-financed tax cuts eventually must be paid for through other taxes, reduced government services, or government borrowing costs — costs that fall broadly on taxpayers rather than on any industry [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is concentrated and easy to name: corporations and their shareholders keep more of their profits. The cost is diffuse: forgone federal revenue with no stated pay-for, which means larger deficits or future tax and service changes borne broadly by the public. The bill as written asks the public to absorb a large, permanent revenue loss with no corresponding benefit spelled out for anyone who does not own corporate stock.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, which never acted on it, so it died there when the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.

narrative.text: Rep. Roger Williams (R-TX) introduced the bill on June 25, 2015, and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day [S1] [S5].
No further action was ever taken: no hearing, no committee markup, no floor vote appears in the bill's complete action history [S5].
The bill drew only two cosponsors, both Republicans [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary taxpayers are no worse off: the Treasury keeps the roughly $1+ trillion in corporate revenue the cut would have forgone over a decade, and no industry gained anything, since the bill never advanced.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The Treasury, and no one else

for.name: Rep. Roger Williams
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to cut the corporate rate to 20% and saw it referred to Ways and Means.

sides.party_line_note: All three supporters named in the record — the sponsor and two cosponsors — were Republicans; no hearing, vote, or recorded opposition ever occurred, so the bill never drew a chamber-wide split.

industries.note: A cut from a 35% top rate to a flat 20% is worth hundreds of billions of dollars a year to the most profitable companies. Because the bill pays for it with nothing — pure deficit increase — the industry's gain is the public's cost. Had it passed, these firms would have been the clear winners.

industries.industry: Small corporations in lower tax brackets
industries.note: Smaller companies that paid rates between 15% and 34% would also pay less, but their savings are proportionally far smaller than those of the largest firms.
